Madam President, South Sudan aligns itself with the African Group and NAM statements and thank the High Commissioner for his oral update. Country-specific mandates should be established with the consent of the country concerned. South Sudan reaffirms its unwavering support to One China principle and its sovereign right to choose independently the path for development in accordance with its national condition. I thank you, Madam Vice-President.
Thank you very much. Next, I give the floor to Lao People's Democratic Republic.

Madam Vice-President, my delegation thanks the High Commissioner for the comprehensive update and congratulates on your reappointment for the second term. Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Ukraine.

Madam President, Several weeks now, Ukrainian cities have been living under an almost continuous threat from Russian drone and missile attacks. Day and night, air raid alarms interrupt ordinary life. People wake up to explosions and go to work between alerts. These attacks do more than destroy homes, energy facilities, railways, and other civilian infrastructure. They disrupt the very fabric of civilian life, as Russia is trying to make fear and insecurity part of the daily routine of millions of Ukrainians. 1st September offered a painful reminder of what this means when Ukrainian children began their new school year not in classrooms, but in bomb shelter. This must never become normal. No child should learn underground because Russia is attacking their cities. No family should plan their days around air raid alerts. Millions of civilians should not live under the constant threat of drones and missiles simply because Russia has chosen to continue its war of aggression. These attacks are not statistics. They are lives interrupted, childhoods stolen, and fundamental human rights violated every single day. We urge this Council to continue calling Russia's violations by the name, demanding accountability, and standing with Ukraine until our people can once again live without fear. I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Uganda.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President.

Uganda aligns with the statement of the NAM and Africa Group. We take note of the High Commissioner's oral update. We share the concerns of the High Commissioner on the increase in conflicts and wars that continue to claim lives and destroy civilian infrastructure in total disregard of international law and multilateralism. The United Nations was created to restore dialogue, multilateralism and peaceful negotiations in respect of territorial borders and national sovereignty. The United Nations, including this Council, must remain committed to this. My government firmly remains committed to the respect of international law and multilateralism in accordance with our international obligations and national laws. Additionally, Uganda will continue to prioritize policies and initiatives that empower our people in key areas, including job creation, education, health, food security, shelter, and water. Finally, I wish to reiterate Uganda's commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights and our readiness to to cooperate with the Council and the Office of the High Commissioner.

I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Rwanda.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President. Rwanda thanks the High Commissioner for his comprehensive global update and aligns itself to the African Group statement. We meet amid growing and increasingly complex conflicts. Accordingly, Rwanda welcomes the emphasis made on prevention, mediation, early warning and technical cooperation. Sustainable peace requires addressing the root causes of conflict, including poverty, exclusion, weak institutions and denial of fundamental rights through prevention, reconciliation, accountability and inclusive development. Rwanda also stresses the need to address emerging challenges, including climate change, disinformation on digital platforms, and the digital divide. These challenges require an effective multilateral collaboration rather than fragmented or politicized responses. In this context, Rwanda denounces the DRC's attempt to politicize the work of this Council and to externalize responsibility for the suffering inflicted upon its citizens and its own actions. The Kinshasa government is responsible for amplifying hate speech. It is responsible for financing armed groups, including the Wazalendo and the FDLR, a UN-sanctioned armed group. Lasting peace requires accountability and genuine commitment to addressing the root causes of conflict. I thank you, Madam Vice-President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Timor-Leste.

Thank you, Madam Vice-Chair. Timor-Leste thanks the High Commissioner for his oral update. At a time of growing conflict, inequality, and humanitarian crisis, Timor-Leste reaffirms that human rights, peace, and sustainable development are inseparable. We must uphold the universality, individuality, and independence of all human rights and ensure that no one is left behind. Timor-Leste places particular emphasis on the human rights dimensions of climate change and environmental degradation, especially for small islands and developing states. Climate change is not only an environmental challenge. It increasingly affects the enjoyment of fundamental rights, including the rights to life, health, food, water, housing, and development. We therefore call for stronger international cooperation, solidarity, and support for countries most vulnerable to these impacts. Technical assistance and capacity building remain essential to strengthen national institutions and advancing the implementation of human rights obligation. Timor-Leste also stresses the importance of protecting civic space and ensuring the meaningful participation of women, children, youth, and persons with disabilities in public life and decision-making. IMO re-affirms its commitment to continue to contribute to dialogue, cooperation and mutual learning. I thank you, Madame Chair.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Argentina.

Thank you, Vice-President. According to the High Commissioner, Our country is one of countries where there is inequality and lack of services with corruption, people living on the streets. Thank you, Madam Vice-President. The United Republic of Tanzania aligns itself with the African Group and takes note of the High Commissioner's global update. We also congratulate the High Commissioner on his appointment and wish him every success in the discharge of his mandate. Amid increasing conflicts and guided by the principles of our foreign policy, we reaffirm our commitment to multilateralism, dialogue, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. In the same spirit, we reiterate our solidarity with the Palestinian people and our support for their right to self-determination and to an independent state. We equally reaffirm the right of the people of Western Sahara to self-determination in accordance with international law. We strongly believe that human rights, peace, and sustainable development are mutually reinforcing and call for international solidarity in advancing the right to development. Nationally, we remain committed to advancing human rights and good governance through continued reforms and stronger institutions. In this spirit, we look forward to our fourth Universal Periodic Review in November as another opportunity for constructive dialogue on our progress, challenges and priorities. The United Republic of Tanzania further remain committed to constructive cooperation with the Office of the High Commissioner and United Nations human rights mechanisms, guided by the principles of universality, objectivity, non-selectivity, dialogue and cooperation with full respect for sovereignty of states. I thank you, Madam Vice-President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Armenia.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. Armenia congratulates the High Commissioner for the renewal of his mandate and wishes him success. We are also thankful for the detailed update. The international human rights system is evolving in a complex context, marked by geopolitical tension, technological transformation and growing pressures on multilateral co-operation. Consensus is becoming difficult, but our commitment to universal principles is more important than ever before. Prevention must remain at the heart of our collective action. Experience has shown the consequences of a lack of swift action in the face of warning signs. Efficient prevention requires emerging risk factors to be heeded and to protect the vulnerable populations and take action before violations spiral. Digital technology, notably AI, are increasingly influencing the exercise of protection of human rights. and it can amplify discrimination and inequalities. This is why Armenia will present, with the members of a small group, a draft project on promotion and protection of the rights of women and girls in the context of digital technology. Technological development must be firmly anchored in international human rights law. President, an international system in human rights must be efficient and meet the, deal with the violations that we're seeing today and anticipate the risks for tomorrow. Thank you, Madam President.

Madam Vice President, the Maldives remains committed to advancing human rights through people-centered and inclusive development. We have undertaken focused efforts to strengthen national mechanisms for the implementation and follow-up of human rights obligations, while enhancing protections and opportunities for women, children, and persons with disabilities. As a SIDS on the front lines of climate crisis, we continue to advance a rights-based approach to climate action as envisaged in our third Nationally Determined Contribution. Madam Vice President, before concluding, I would like to make the following observations. The Maldives also recognizes the progress made by Sri Lanka in advancing national reconciliation and the promotion and protection of human rights. We underscore the importance of continued constructive engagement with OHCHR and human rights mechanisms, complemented by international support. I thank you.

I thank you. That was the last speaker on my list. We shall now turn to the list of speakers for national human rights institutions and non-governmental organizations. First, I give the floor to Coordination des associations et des particuliers pour la liberté de conscience.

We, along with Human Rights Without Frontiers, are deeply concerned about grave violation of international, humanitarian, and human rights law in Sudan and their devastating impact on civilians. We urge urgent action on allegation that the Sudanese army forces use chemical agents. France 24 investigation, echoed by Human Rights Watch, documents chlorine attacks near Al-Jali refinery. These warrants prompt impartial and independent scrutiny. Investigation must preserve evidence, protect witnesses, and establish responsibility. We are also alarmed by the protection situation in El Obeid. Reports indicate restriction of movement, impeded access, and allegation that civilians are prevented from leaving safely by the Sudanese army forces. These claims require investigations. All parties must guarantee safe passage, facilitate humanitarian access, and respect the civilian characters of homes, hospitals, and schools. We welcome the Security Council recognition of regional peace efforts. External military logistical and financial support that may contribute to violations must face scrutiny. States with influence, including Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Turkey, should disclose assistance and cooperate with inquiries. The Council must strengthen monitoring and protect civilians and ensure accountability without delay. I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Midline for Human Rights.

Mr. President. Midline for Human Rights welcomes the continued engagement of the fact-finding mission on the deteriorating human rights situation in Sudan. The suffering of Sudanese civilians is intolerable. Communities in Darfur and elsewhere continue to face killings, displacement, sexual violence, destruction of homes and essential services, arbitrary detention, torture, and obstruction of humanitarian assistance. Recent UN information also documents grave allegations concerning RSF detention facilities and the treatment of civilians in El Fasher. The Council should strengthen the fact-finding mission's capacity to investigate and preserve evidence, support accountability through the International Criminal Court, expand targeted sanctions against those responsible for atrocities, and address external military and financial support that enables violations. We further call for safe and unhindered humanitarian access and effective protection of civilians. Sudan does not need more statements of concern. Sudan needs decisive international action to protect civilians and end impunity. Thank you.

Madam Vice-President, We thank the High Commissioner and his staff at the Sri Lanka Accountability Project for their work towards accountability for international crimes committed during and after Sri Lanka's civil war. Tamils are grateful for their efforts at bringing to light what Tamils consider genocide:

the decades-long effort by the Sri Lankan state to direct

violence at the Tamil community to weaken and even destroy Tamil

physical, cultural, and economic presence on the island of Sri Lanka. We note that in Resolution 30/1, an international role in domestic accountability was mandated by the Council agreed to by Sri Lanka. Since such a justice mechanism with international participation has never been established, High Commissioners began recommending international forms of justice such as universal jurisdiction.

Sri Lanka is incapable of prosecuting crimes by itself through purely

domestic mechanisms, and unless justice is dispensed, human rights will forever be in danger in Sri Lanka, especially for Tamil and other non-Sinhalese Buddhists. We are disappointed that Member States and others have not taken action based on the High Commissioner's recommendation. recommendations and strongly urge all states to start prosecution in the coming year. We urge member states to take advantage of other international avenues for justice such as the ICJ, the ICC,

and a standalone judicial mechanism.

Today, we draw attention to the emblematic cases of the mass graves

at Chenmay and Manad, which require international attention, and we thank Ana Lorena Delgado

Perez of the Working Group on Involuntary or Enforced Disappearances for her visit. Thank you for your time.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Physicians for Human Rights.

Physicians for Human Rights and the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa express our grave concern at the deepening human rights crisis in

Ethiopia, where violence continues to spread across regions nearly four years after the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement in the absence of meaningful justice.

CHR and OCHA have documented widespread, systematic, and

deliberate acts of conflict-related sexual and reproductive violence, including rape, forced pregnancy, and forced witnessing of sexual violence. Health workers in Tigray treated survivors whose attackers expressed intent to destroy their ability to reproduce. Similar patterns of sexual and reproductive violence also occurred in Amhara and Afar, in part fueled by impunity. We have also found that attacks on healthcare continue and have become normalized across conflict settings, implicating every major armed party.

Attacks have destroyed and disabled health facilities, stripped systems of critical supplies,

harmed health workers, and left patients without access to essential care, just as health systems are weakened further by global health funding cuts. Meanwhile, independent oversight has collapsed. Three years ago, ICRI's mandate was not renewed, and OHCHR has not issued a public report on Ethiopia since 2024.

Human rights defenders and health workers who witness these abuses face growing risks in reporting.

We urge the High

Commissioner to resume regular public reporting on the human rights situation in Ethiopia, and the Human Rights Council must do more to ensure credible human rights monitoring and independent documentation of crimes in Ethiopia.

Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Promotion du Developpement Economique et Social.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. We thank the High Commissioner for his update and for reaffirming that prevention and effective protection remain at the heart of the international human rights system responsibilities. Experience has shown that the most difficult challenges facing this system are not limited to crises. that command the attention of the international community. They also arise in situations that persist for so long that the exception risks becoming the norm, the prolonged suffering risks gradually becoming perceived as ordinary. In this context, protracted humanitarian situations should not become protection blind spots. While humanitarian assistance remains indispensable, it cannot substitute the safeguards required to protect individual rights, nor independent monitoring, nor effective access to complaint and redress mechanisms. It is for this reason that we would like to draw the attention of the Council to the situation of the population living in the Tandoof camps, where the persistence over several decades of humanitarian and protection concerns call for a shift from the long-term management to effective and sustainable protection. The situation highlights the importance of the responsibility of all relevant parties, each within the scope of their respective obligations and competencies, the host in particular, bears the responsibility to ensure an environment that respects the fundamental rights of persons present on its territory to facilitate their access to complaint mechanisms and to enable cooperation with the UN mechanisms and independent monitoring processes. Thank you, Madam Vice President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Rezo Africain pour le Developpement, la Gouvernance et les Droits de l'Homme.

Madam Vice-President, I am addressing you today as a former Sahrawi detainee who suffered enforced disappearance and torture in a Polisario secret centre in Tindouf. I want to draw your attention to the serious deterioration of the human rights situation in the Sahrawi refugee camps, where the Polisario leadership exploits the legal vacuum to commit heinous crimes against those who dare to speak out. We've seen extrajudicial killings, abductions and torture, and exploitation of children. So our children in the tent of camps have seen their rights violated. They're separated from their families at an early age to be transferred to another country. in order to indoctrinate them with political and cultural principles that are foreign to their culture and religion. They have military training imposed upon them, including the use of firearms and explosives, which has led to the death of many of them in some Latin American countries, where they lost their lives. Sometimes They were buried according to rituals that do not belong to their Islamic religion. Syrian children are also exposed in other ways. They are placed in families and so-called holiday camps.

I would ask all speakers to deliver their statements in a reasonable pace to allow the interpreters also to do their job. So next, I give the floor to Institut International pour les Droits et le Developpement.

The IRDG presents before you the findings of its report on the UAE role in the Sudanese conflict, based on cross-verification of over 30 reliable sources, a correlation, and a counterfactual analysis. Findings indicate a sustained Emirati role, enabling RSF to maintain military capacity, in clear violation of the arms embargo, the UN Charter, and IHL. Verified arms transfers under humanitarian cover, financial flows, and logistical coordination confirm an organized and continuous system of support. The statistical analysis reveals a strong correlation, as the major RSF-held territory covers gold-producing regions, controlling now 90% of the production, and directly benefiting UAE gold trade, increasingly dependent on Sudanese supply. The counterfactual analysis confirms a causal relationship. When Emirati support was disrupted due to war, RSF performance declined and lost ground. It shows that RSF depends structurally on the UAE backing. The volume and quality of verified evidence can no longer be ignored and surpasses any diplomatic denial. We therefore urge the immediate establishment of a UN investigation into the UAE intervention and sustained diplomatic pressure to sever all support channels to the RSF. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Global Sri Lankan Forum, United Kingdom.

Madam Vice President, we raise grave concern over severe and compounding threats facing individual liberty, the rule of law, and vital checks and balances in Sri Lanka. Executive overreach is systematically undermining the foundational value upon which the Republic was built. Political victimization and selective prosecution are evident through targeted arrest of opposition figures like Namal Rajapaksa. This is compounded by the continued detention of former SIS Director Suresh Sali, highlighting persistent gaps in judicial oversight and due process. Such arbitrary detention Practices directly inflame severe prison overcrowding where recent fatal riots expose inhuman conditions threatening all inmates. Systematic risks extend further with the 22nd Constitutional Amendment altering sitting judges' retirement age mid-tenure, compromising judicial independence and interfering with the administration of justice. As warned by the UN Special Rapporteur and the Bar Association of Sri Lanka, this creates executive patronage. The Commonwealth Lawyers Association also noted severe procedural flaws when petitioners were denied full hearing and refusal their right to oral reply. Similarly, Anti-Corruption Act amendments grant the Director General power via certificate to restrict bail, enforcing prolonged pretrial detention. Ultimately, these cumulative measures pose a direct threat to dissent and freedom of expression, particularly targeting social media journalists. We call upon this Council and the High Commissioner to maintain active oversight over Sri Lanka. Thank you, Madam Vice-President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Society for Development and Community Empowerment.

Madam Vice President and distinguished members of the Council, we express our sincere appreciation to the United Nations Human Rights Council and its human rights mechanism for their continued attention to the murder case of K. Amstrung and their concern regarding accountability and the protection of the human rights defender. Mr. K. Amstrung was a prominent political leader in Tamil Nadu, a lawyer, a strong advocate for equality, social justice, and the right of marginalized communities. Through legal, political, and community work, he supported disadvantaged communities and created opportunities for young people and aspiring lawyers. On July 4, 2024, Mr. Amstang was assassinated in broad daylight in Chennai. His killing raises serious concerns not only about individual criminal responsibility but also about the safety of human rights defenders, lawyers, and marginalized communities. Madam President, accountability must extend to the entire chain of responsibility. The investigation must establish who planned, financed, facilitated, or ordered the including by the credible allegation involving influential political, police or any business figures. No one should escape investigation because of political influence, official position or wealth. We appreciate the action taken by the Tamil Nadu State Government, Honorable Chief Minister, Mr. Joseph Vijay, and the PWD Minister, Mr. Adhivajuna, in supporting strong action and investigation. We urge the United Nations to continue the monitoring this case and request the relevant special rapporteur and special procedure to closely follow the CBI investigation, ensuring that it remains independent, impartial, and effective. Justice for Mr. Amstrong. Jai Bhim. Thank you, ma'am.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Eastern Horn of Africa Human Rights Defenders Project.

Madam Vice-President, we thank the High Commissioner and stress the importance of his global mandate. Through it and OHCHR's inquiries branch, he plays an important role in addressing situations not addressed by the Council. Nowhere is the High Commissioner's voice more strategic. One case in point is Ethiopia. Three years ago, the Council discontinued ICHR's mandate. We reiterate the need to correct that mistake by reinstating a mechanism on Ethiopia. We urge OHCHR to resume its public reporting on the country, where conflicts are raging, the crackdown on civic space is intensifying, and the transitional justice process is stalled. We are deeply concerned about the risk of a renewed conflict in the Horn of Africa. Madam President, the Council's 20th anniversary is an opportunity for reflection. Investigative mechanisms are created, they report on violations, then are discontinued. Often, no follow-up mechanism is mandated. As attacks on multilateralism multiply and double standards fuel cynicism, the question is, what should the Council do to maintain attention to and advance accountability for crimes committed in countries such as Eritrea or Burundi? We know the worst option, giving up and letting crisis slip out of the agenda. We do not know the best, but more than ever, we must make the case for human rights to play a role in solving crisis, ensuring justice, and building sustainable peace. I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to International Federation on Aging.

President. The International Federation on Ageing welcomes the High Commissioner's oral update and his continued leadership on the human rights of all people. As populations age in every region, older persons must be equally and explicitly protected by the international human rights system. The Human Rights Council's decision to begin elaborating a legally binding instrument on the rights of older persons is a significant step towards closing long-standing gaps in protection. Its value, however, will ultimately be measured by whether it changes the lived experience of older people. This means a strong, comprehensive instrument that addresses age discrimination and ageism, protects autonomy and independence, advances the rights to health and long-term care, and safeguards the right of older persons to participate fully in their communities and societies. It also means ensuring that older persons are meaningfully involved throughout the process. President, we urge the High Commissioner, Member States and civil society to sustain momentum and ambition as this work proceeds. Older persons have waited too long for their rights to be made explicit. The international community now has both the opportunity and the responsibility to ensure those rights are protected for generations to come. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Africa Culture International.

Madam Vice-President, in Africa, the vulnerability of children remains a major concern. More worrying still, there are some initiatives that are presented as humanitarian that can transform this vulnerability into an instrument or a tool to serve political or ideological interests. Africa Culture International would like to draw your attention to the programme that's called Holidays in Peace, This organises every year the displacement of Sahrawi children abroad, principally in Spain, dressed up as a humanitarian holiday. This raises the question of the political instrumentalisation of these children and transparency as to their selection, placement and their hosts. The lack of independent guarantees compels us to examine the risks of exploitation and practices that can also be tantamount to people trafficking. Programmes that are dressed up as humanitarian programmes should not promote breaking away from language, identity, cultural practices and family ties. Africa Culture International calls on the High Commissioner and competent mechanisms to review independently the purpose, operations and guarantees surrounding this programme. Humanitarian action must protect children and not be used as a way of instrumentalising them or erasing their identity.
I thank you.

Madam Vice-President, we thank the High Commissioner for his update. We remain gravely concerned by the worsening human rights situation in occupied Western Sahara, where Sahrawi civilians, including human rights defenders and journalists, are subjected to surveillance, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment and repression of fundamental freedoms. As noted by the Secretary General in his report on the situation concerning Western Sahara, the absence of independent, impartial, comprehensive and sustained human rights monitoring continues to undermine the accurate assessment of development on the ground. The report further notes that the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights has been unable to access Western Sahara despite repeated requests, perpetuating a significant monitoring and protection gap. Recent findings by the United Nations Human Rights Mechanism have further highlighted the importance of accountability and the protection of fundamental rights. Across these cases, violations of the Convention against Torture, including failure to investigate allegations of torture and the use of statements allegedly obtained under torture in criminal proceedings, have been founded. The persistent lack of independent monitoring and the denial of access to UN mechanisms, including your office and special procedures, contribute to an alarming culture of impunity and information blackout. We are equally alarmed by the illegal exploitation of Western Sahara's natural resources in violation of international law and continue continued forcible displacement and evictions of Sahrawis to benefit the occupier. We urge your office to renew its efforts to gain access to the territory and to reaffirm the rights of the Sahrawi people to self-determination. This is not optional. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Organization for Defending Victims of Violence.

Mr. President, the High Commissioner's report calls for peace, respect for human rights, and the international rule of law. Yet the US aggression against Iran stands in stark contrast to these principles. This aggression is a destabilizing, multilayered operation. One layer, military attacks killing civilians, leaders and commanders, school children, oil and energy infrastructure, and another layer, an economic warfare machine that undermines the human rights of the Iranian people. Rather than advancing peace and international law, the United States has compounded the suffering of civilians through the combined use of military force and economic coercion. The US threatened genocide and total annihilation of Iran. What remained is a strategy of chaos, aimless, global harming, and still burning. Mr. President, we call on the UN High Commissioner to establish an independent UN mechanism to investigate the attacks against civilians and civilian objects, preserve evidence, identify perpetrators, and bring them to justice, especially for the double attack at the Mina Primary School and attack on Lomer Sports Hall. The latter killed child athletes and severely injured over 100 civilians with its 720,000 phosphorus-coated tungsten pellets. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Al-Bashir Foundation for Development. Next, I give the floor to Asian Forum for Human Rights and Development.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President. We welcome the High Commissioner's report and its call for robust accountability and institutional reforms in Sri Lanka. The National People's Power government came to office with considerable hope and expectation of a genuine break from the cycles of impunity and repression. Yet, two years on, there has been little meaningful progress on accountability. Apart from limited progress in a few emblematic cases, there has been no progress on others, such as enforced disappearances, the killing of aid workers, and attacks against journalists. Longstanding commitments, including to establish a judicial mechanism with international participation and to implement legal and institutional reforms have also not materialized. Civic space is likewise under pressure. In the north and the east, surveillance and intimidation of journalists, activists, families of the disappeared, and human rights defenders continue. Peaceful protests and memorialization continue to face scrutiny and intimidation. Despite the government's promise to repeal the Draconian Prevention of Terrorism Act, the law continues to be used to arrest and detain people. The proposed NGO registration and supervision bill raises further alarm. Rather than protecting independent civil society, it will expand state control of NGOs. We urge the government to withdraw the bill entirely. The government came to office promising to break with the past. It must now demonstrate that this was a genuine commitment to change. Until these commitments become reality, the Council and the OHCHR must continue scrutiny. I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to World Evangelical Alliance.

Ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen. At the same time, identified some areas where further efforts are needed, such as remaining protection gaps affecting migrants, persons with disabilities and trans persons. Particular attention should be given to family reunification procedures and to the use of solitary confinement, especially for migrants in pre-trial detention. I also note with concern recent amendments to the Foreign National Acts especially the abolition of the 18-month rule and the introduction of broader grounds for revoking international protection. Finally, I call for stronger safeguards concerning involuntary psychiatric treatment and welcome recent efforts to address gender-based violence. Overall, Iceland demonstrates how a small nation can exercise meaningful global leadership in advancing human rights. I close with a commitment to multipolarity embedded in the United Nations Charter. Sovereignty, development, democracy, and human rights are not rival principles. They are and must remain complementary. I thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr. Katrougalos, for this presentation. Excellencies, distinguished participants, this brings us to the end of this meeting. I wish to thank interpreters for their flexibility and according us 10 extra minutes tonight. We will reconvene tomorrow morning at 10:00 a.m. to continue interactive dialogue with the independent expert on the promotion of a democratic and equitable international order, followed by the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on the negative impact of unilateral coercive measures on the enjoyment of human rights. I hereby close the fourth meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council.
